"Fighting slump: A CIO's game of," dated April 30, 2009.

The city of the Republic, as envisioned by Plato, is characterized by a unique property system and a community of wives for the guardians, as well as the absence of written law. This societal structure includes common meals and gymnasia, which, while beneficial in many ways, can become dangerous in the event of civil strife, as evidenced by the cases of the youth in Miletus, Boeotia, and Thurii. Furthermore, Plato argues that long-standing institutions may corrupt natural pleasures of love, which are shared not only by humans but also by animals. He holds the states, particularly those that encourage the use of gymnasia, primarily responsible for this corruption. The pleasure derived from same-sex relationships is seen as contrary to nature, according to Plato. He accuses the Cretans of fabricating the story of Ganymede to justify their "unnatural pleasures." The Republic is a dialogue between Socrates and several young men, exploring various aspects of an ideal society. In contrast, the Laws is a discussion among three elderly men who devise a strategy for reproductive law, aiming to conceal their rhetorical tactics of piety, rituals, and virtue from the younger generation. Plato acknowledges the existence of a device for this law, as he states, "I know of a device for this law." In summary, the city of the Republic, as described by Plato, is a complex society with unique institutions and values. While it aims to create an ideal state, it also faces potential challenges and criticisms, particularly regarding its approach to love and relationships.

The term "corner office" is often associated with prestige and power in a professional setting. It typically refers to the office space located at the corner of a building, which is usually reserved for high-ranking executives or senior managers. The phrase has been used in various contexts, reflecting its significance in the corporate world. American Public Media's "Marketplace" radio program features a segment called "Conversations from the Corner Office," where CEOs from different industries share their insights and experiences. This recurring segment highlights the importance of leadership and decision-making in various sectors. Richard Conniff, in his book "Ape in the Corner Office," explores the application of evolutionary biology and sociobiology theories to management concepts in the workplace. The book delves into the behavioral patterns and dynamics that can be observed in office environments, drawing parallels with the natural world. In the entertainment industry, the term "corner office" has also made its way into popular culture. For instance, the law-drama series "Suits" frequently references the corner office, emphasizing the status and influence that come with occupying such a space. The series showcases the competitive nature of the legal profession and the desire to reach the top. Additionally, "Corner Office" is a 2022 black comedy film directed by Joachim Back and starring Jon Hamm. The film's narrative revolves around the concept of the corner office, further emphasizing its symbolic value in the corporate world. The phrase "corner office" has also been used in music, with "Corner Office Bedroom" being a song by the band PlayRadioPlay!. This demonstrates the widespread recognition and cultural impact of the term. In literature, the concept of the corner office has been explored in various books. Dr. Lois P. Frankel's "Nice Girls Don't Get the Corner Office: 101 Unconscious Mistakes Women Make That Sabotage Their Careers" discusses the challenges faced by women in the corporate world and the unconscious biases that can hinder their progress. The book provides valuable advice for women seeking to advance their careers and break the glass ceiling. Furthermore, David Leonhardt's article "Who's in the Corner Office?" published in The New York Times, delves into the characteristics and qualities of individuals who occupy these prestigious positions. The article examines the factors that contribute to their success and the responsibilities they hold. Valerie Young's "The Secret Thoughts of Successful Women" also touches upon the topic, discussing the mindset and strategies that have helped women achieve success in their careers. The book provides an in-depth look at the thought processes and behaviors that contribute to professional growth. In summary, the "corner office" is a term that has permeated various aspects of society, from business and management to entertainment and literature. It symbolizes the pinnacle of professional achievement and the desire to reach the top of the corporate ladder.

The Association for Law, Property, and Society is a scholarly organization in the United States dedicated to the study of property law and its social implications. Established to foster research and dialogue in this field, the association brings together academics, professionals, and students. One of the primary activities of the association is organizing an annual conference. The inaugural edition of this conference was held at Georgetown Law in 2010, marking the beginning of a tradition that continues to provide a platform for the exchange of ideas and scholarly debate. In addition to the conference, the Association for Law, Property, and Society is also the publisher of the academic journal "Law, Property and Society." This journal serves as a forum for the dissemination of research findings and scholarly articles that contribute to the understanding of property law and its intersection with societal issues. As of the latest update, the leadership of the association is held by Tim Mulvaney, who is a faculty member at Texas A&M University. His role as president involves overseeing the organization's activities and ensuring its continued relevance and contribution to the field of property law and society studies. The Association for Law, Property, and Society plays a vital role in advancing the understanding of property law and its impact on society, providing a valuable resource for those interested in this area of legal scholarship.

This paper introduces the concept of the implied Sharpe ratio, a novel measure of a European option's attractiveness to an investor. The Sharpe ratio, traditionally used to evaluate mutual fund performance, has been adapted here to assess the value of options within an investment portfolio. The paper builds upon seminal works by Sharpe, Jensen, Merton, and others, who have explored the performance of investment portfolios and the impact of risk on asset returns. The implied Sharpe ratio is defined in relation to the Merton value function, which represents the maximum expected utility of an investor's wealth under the assumption of a geometric Brownian motion for the risky asset. The implied Sharpe ratio is the unique positive solution that equates the investor's value function in a general market setting with the Merton value function. This innovative concept allows investors to evaluate European options based on their potential to enhance expected terminal utility, rather than relying solely on implied volatility, which does not capture an option's worth relative to an investor's utility. The equation for the ratio in terms of model parameters and an investor's risk-aversion is derived from the paper. Using a Taylor series expansion technique, the authors develop semi-explicit approximations of the implied Sharpe ratio, facilitating its calculation under various local stochastic volatility models. The authors demonstrate the practical application of the implied Sharpe ratio through examples, highlighting its utility in identifying the most suitable European option for investment among available choices. The paper's contribution lies in providing investors with a new tool for assessing the value of European options in the context of their overall investment strategy, taking into account the investor's risk preferences and the specific characteristics of the options under consideration.

In December 1980, the concept of Special Assistance Resource Teachers was introduced, which aimed to identify and address literacy and numeracy deficits in individual children. This approach was supported by various major committees of inquiry and their respective reports. Key reports that influenced this educational philosophy include: 1. The Bullock Report (1975) - A UK Committee of Inquiry appointed by the Secretary of State for Education and Science. 2. The Cadman Report (1976) - A report by the Australian Parliament's House of Representatives Select Committee on Specific Learning Difficulties. 3. The 1977 Report of the Working Party on Provisions for Children with Special Needs in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT). 4. The Warnock Report (1978) - A UK Committee of Inquiry into the Education of Handicapped Children and Young People. 5. Task Force 8's Report was submitted to the Victorian State Council for Special Education. 6. The Victorian Ministerial Committee on Special Assistance Programs' Report (1980). The educational philosophy that underpinned the Special Assistance Program was deeply rooted in these reports. It emphasized the significant impact of a child's learning environment on their behavior and learning. Furthermore, it recognized the importance of meeting children's learning needs within a shared structural and social framework. This perspective led to the development of programs that provided resources and assistance to classroom teachers, enabling them to better support students with specific learning challenges.

Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) is a mandatory health insurance scheme for international students studying in Australia, as stipulated by the Australian Government. The coverage of this insurance is similar to the Australian Medicare system, meaning that students have access to necessary healthcare services while in the country. International students have the option to arrange their OSHC payments through their educational institution. However, they are not restricted to the institution's recommended provider. Students can independently select an OSHC provider of their choice, even if the institution has a preferred provider arrangement with a specific insurer. Only Australian private health insurers who have entered into a Deed with the Australian government are authorized to offer OSHC. This Deed outlines the essential conditions that registered insurers must meet to provide the OSHC product. As a legal agreement between the Commonwealth of Australia and the respective insurer, the Deed specifies the minimum benefits that must be covered by the insurer. It also delineates the circumstances under which the insurer is exempt from providing benefits. Furthermore, clause 6.8 of the Deed outlines the conditions under which insurers can terminate policies and issue refunds. These conditions include: 1. If a student decides not to come to Australia. 2. If a student has ceased their studies and left Australia before the expiration of their visa. 3. If a student's application for an extended stay is denied by the Department of Home Affairs. The OSHC is designed to ensure that international students have access to healthcare services while in Australia, providing peace of mind and financial protection during their studies.

A school uniform is a standardized attire worn by students, primarily in educational institutions such as schools. These uniforms are prevalent in primary and secondary schools across various countries. A typical school uniform may include button-down shirts, trousers for boys, and blouses, pleated skirts for girls, along with blazers for both genders. Alternatively, uniforms can be as simple as mandating collared shirts, limiting color choices, or restricting the types of clothing items students are allowed to wear. There is a distinction between dress codes and school uniforms. According to scholars like Nathan Joseph, clothing can only be considered a uniform if it (a) serves as a group emblem, (b) certifies an institution's legitimacy by revealing individuals' relative positions, and (c) suppresses individuality. In contrast, a dress code is less restrictive and focuses on promoting modesty and discouraging anti-social fashion statements, as noted by Marian Wilde. Dress codes may include rules such as prohibiting ripped clothing, disallowing logos, or limiting the amount of exposed skin. School uniforms are specific to each educational level, with each institution often having its own unique design. The history of school uniforms is not easily traced, as there is no single comprehensive written account. However, it is believed that the practice of wearing uniforms in schools has a long-standing tradition with various known influences.

Our study looked at the nature of profit landscapes in financial markets, comparing real market data with various artificial time series models. The scaling behavior of the number of local maxima, $M$, with respect to the resolution parameter, $N$, follows a power-law relationship. Intriguingly, real market data exhibits a scaling exponent $a \approx 1.6$, which is not replicated by models with short-tailed return distributions such as Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM) and Fractional Brownian Motion (FBM). The Log-Periodic Power Law (LP) and Multifractal Superposition Model (MSM) successfully reproduce the observed scaling exponent. Notably, our analysis of the LP model reveals that the heavy-tail of the return distribution is the primary driver of the fractality observed in the profit landscape. Our research also explores the maximum attainable value of the scaling exponent $a$ within the MSM, suggesting a potential upper limit of $a \approx 1.6$. This intriguing observation opens avenues for future studies to understand the underlying reasons for this behavior. Additionally, we demonstrate that the fractal nature of the profit landscape is largely independent of long-term memory effects in the time series, as evidenced by the preservation of the scaling exponent even after shuffling the time series to eliminate long-term correlations. The heavy-tail of the return distribution is identified as the key factor contributing to the fractality in the profit landscape, a finding that has significant implications for the validation of artificial time series models for stock prices. By adjusting model parameters, such as $\alpha$ in LP and $m_0$ in MSM, researchers can align the fractality of artificial time series with that observed in real markets, thereby enhancing the models' realism and predictive capabilities. In conclusion, our work highlights the importance of heavy-tailed return distributions in financial markets and their role in shaping the fractal characteristics of profit landscapes. This insight can guide the development of more accurate and reliable models for financial time series analysis. The National Research Foundation of Korea helped facilitate this research.

The importance of understanding human rights and the programs implemented to protect them cannot be overstated. Education plays a pivotal role in this context, as it aims to inform beneficiaries about their human rights and the efforts made by non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and other entities to enhance these rights. Education helps to educate governments, international organizations, and donor agencies about their responsibilities in protecting human rights. One of the key principles in this domain is the right to participation. This principle emphasizes the importance of including beneficiaries in the planning and implementation of programs designed to benefit them. By involving beneficiaries, organizations can empower them and ensure that their needs and perspectives are taken into account. Accountability is a crucial principle. This principle establishes standards for human rights and development, holding NGOs, international organizations, donor agencies, and governments to higher standards of responsibility. Accountability ensures that these entities are transparent, efficient, and effective in their efforts to promote and protect human rights. Several NGOs have been traditionally involved in advocating for human rights. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch are two such organizations that have expanded their focus from political rights to include economic and social rights as well. This expansion reflects the growing recognition of the interconnectedness of various types of rights and the need for a comprehensive approach to human rights advocacy. A rights-based approach to development has been adopted by Oxfam. This organization has committed to not only providing relief to those in need but also addressing the structural causes of poverty and injustice. By doing so, Oxfam aims to tackle the root causes of these issues and create lasting, sustainable change. This approach integrates poverty, human rights, development, and trade within the same framework, reflecting a holistic and comprehensive understanding of the challenges faced by marginalized communities. In conclusion, the promotion and protection of human rights require a multifaceted approach that includes education, participation, and accountability. NGOs play a vital role in this process, advocating for the rights of individuals and communities and working towards a more just and equitable world. By adopting rights-based approaches, these organizations can effectively address the complex issues surrounding human rights and development.

The Wallace Clark Award, also known as the Wallace Clark Medal, was a prestigious honor bestowed upon individuals for their Distinguished Contribution to Scientific Management. This accolade was named in honor of Henry Wallace Clark (1880-1948), a prominent figure in the field of scientific management. Established in 1949, the award was supported by several renowned organizations, including the American Management Association (AMA), the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME), the Association for Consulting Management Engineers, and the Society for the Advancement of Management. These organizations recognized the importance of scientific management and its impact on various industries. The first recipient of the Wallace Clark Medal was Swiss Hugo de Haan in 1948. At the time, de Haan held the position of executive secretary for the Comite International de l'Organisation Scientifique (CIOS). CIOS was an organization dedicated to promoting scientific management globally. It was founded during the first International Management Congress in Prague in 1924, which aimed to foster the advancement of management practices worldwide. The Wallace Clark Award celebrated the achievements of individuals who made significant contributions to the field of scientific management. Strategic planning is a critical process for organizations, focusing on the development and implementation of long-term goals and objectives. It involves a comprehensive analysis of the current business environment, the identification of potential opportunities and threats, and the formulation of strategies to achieve desired outcomes. One key aspect of strategic planning is the concept of "strategic windows," which emphasizes the importance of timing in the execution of strategies. The entrance and exit points of a strategy must be considered carefully. This concept has led some strategic planners to incorporate planned obsolescence into their strategies, allowing for the natural evolution and replacement of strategies over time. In 1983, Noel Tichy highlighted the challenges of habitual thinking in strategic planning. He argued that our natural tendency to repeat familiar patterns can limit creativity, hinder the exploration of new ideas, and impede our ability to address complex issues. To overcome these challenges, Tichy proposed a systematic approach to change that involves examining new issues from three perspectives: technical and production, political and resource allocation, and corporate culture. Charles Handy, in 1989, identified two types of change in organizations: "strategic drift" and "transformational change." Strategic drift refers to a gradual change that occurs so subtly that it often goes unnoticed until it is too late. On the other hand, transformational change is sudden and radical, typically triggered by significant disruptions or external shocks in the business environment. Andy Grove, in the same year, introduced the term "strategic inflection point" to describe the moment when a new trend or direction is initiated. These inflection points can be either subtle or radical, depending on the nature of the change. Richard Pascale, in 1990, emphasized the need for continuous reinvention in the face of relentless change. He suggested that past successes can become the source of future weaknesses if organizations become too reliant on them. This highlights the importance of constantly adapting and evolving strategies to stay ahead in a dynamic business landscape. In summary, strategic planning is a complex and ongoing process that requires organizations to be agile, innovative, and adaptable. By understanding the concepts of strategic windows, planned obsolescence, and the different types of change, organizations can better navigate the challenges of a rapidly changing business environment and ensure their long-term success.

The article discusses the integration of information technology in higher education, highlighting various initiatives and their impact on learning experiences. This initiative demonstrated the potential of technology to enhance educational experiences. The Universal Life Church (ULC) is a religious organization that offers online ordination to individuals who wish to become ministers. These ministers are then able to perform various religious ceremonies, including marriage. The ULC's ministers are recognized in several states across the United States, and the laws regarding their authority to solemnize marriages vary from state to state. In Alaska, marriages can be solemnized by a minister, priest, or rabbi of any church or congregation within the state, or by the principal officer or elder of recognized churches or congregations that traditionally do not have regular ministers, priests, or rabbis. Additionally, marriages can be performed before or in any religious organization or congregation according to the established ritual or form commonly practiced in the organization or congregation. As of 2011, no court or administrative ruling in Alaska had excluded those ordained as ministers of the ULC. In Arizona, individuals authorized to solemnize marriages include duly licensed or ordained clergymen. As of 2011, no court or administrative ruling in Arizona had excluded those ordained as ministers of the ULC. Arkansas law allows for the solemnization of marriage by any regularly ordained minister or priest of any religious sect or denomination. As of 2011, no court or administrative ruling in Arkansas had excluded those ordained as ministers of the ULC. In California, a marriage may be solemnized by a priest, minister, rabbi, or authorized person. The specific requirements for authorization may vary, but the ULC's ministers are recognized in the state. It is always advisable to consult with local authorities or legal experts to ensure compliance with current laws and regulations, as the recognition of ULC ministers and their authority to perform marriages can change over time.

Asynchronous learning has a rich history dating back to the late 19th century, when formalized correspondence education, also known as distance learning, first utilized the postal system to include physically remote learners in educational opportunities. This marked the beginning of a new era in education, allowing students to learn independently and at their own pace. The 1920s and 1930s brought about significant advancements in the field, with the introduction of recorded audio. This development desynchronized broadcasting and greatly enhanced the mass dissemination of information. It allowed educational content to reach a wider audience, breaking the barriers of time and location. A major milestone in the distribution of standardized educational content occurred during World War II. The US military branches produced hundreds of training films, which were screened millions of times, ensuring that soldiers received consistent and standardized education regardless of their location. The advent of online asynchronous learning can be traced back to the early 1980s when schools and universities began investing in computer technology. Pioneering applications such as Seymour Papert's Logo programming language enabled students to learn at their own pace, without being confined to the synchronous constraints of a traditional classroom lecture. As computers became more accessible and schools started connecting to the emerging Internet, asynchronous learning networks began to take shape. These networks supplemented existing classroom learning and gave rise to a new correspondence model for solitary learners. Students could now access online resources and communicate asynchronously through email and discussion boards. The 1990s saw the emergence of telecampuses, with universities offering courses and degree programs through a combination of asynchronous and synchronous online instruction. This marked a significant shift in the way education was delivered, making it more flexible and accessible to a broader range of learners. With the integration of advanced multimedia technologies, asynchronous learning has evolved further. These innovations have enhanced the learning experience, providing students with a wealth of resources and tools to facilitate independent learning and collaboration, regardless of their geographical location or time constraints.

Business schools often have different criteria for admission to their MBA programs, and entrance exam scores are not always required. Instead, these institutions aim to create a diverse class by considering factors such as the target male-female ratio and the balance between local and international students. In some rare cases, an undergraduate degree is not mandatory for MBA admission, and significant management experience can be accepted as an alternative. For instance, in the UK, a Higher National Diploma (HND) or a Higher National Certificate (HNC) is considered acceptable by some programs. Work experience is a critical component of the admissions process for many MBA programs. The type and duration of work experience can significantly influence an applicant's chances of admission. Top-tier programs typically require applicants to have at least five or more years of work experience. The United States is home to a growing number of prospective MBA applicants. In 2016 as many as one-quarter of applicants used these services, and their popularity is growing in other countries. These consultants offer a range of services, such as assistance with program selection, mock interviews, and essay proofreading. Some even provide more comprehensive services, like writing essays from scratch. However, the use of consulting services is often viewed unfavorably by admissions committees at many business schools. Applications may be negatively impacted if they appear to have been written with the help of a consultant. This can happen if the writing quality is significantly higher than the candidate's spoken language or if the application lacks uniqueness. It is essential for applicants to present their genuine skills and experiences in their applications to increase their chances of admission to MBA programs.

The Higher Education Act was enacted in 2004. 8) is a piece of legislation passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, which significantly reformed the higher education system in the UK, particularly in England and Wales. The Act's most notable and contentious provisions pertain to changes in university funding and the implementation of tuition fees. It is important to note that university funding is under the jurisdiction of Northern Ireland and Scotland, and is therefore not affected by the Act. The Act was the culmination of extensive and often heated debates. It received Royal Assent on 1st July 2004. Prior to 1998, higher education in the UK, including university courses, was tuition-free. However, the Labour Party, under the leadership of Prime Minister Tony Blair, abolished the student maintenance grant system and introduced an upfront fee of over £1,000 per year for all university students. While a portion of this fee was waived for the most financially disadvantaged students, critics argued that this move would burden students with unnecessary debt and detract from the principle of free public education. The government maintained that the introduction of fees was essential for adequately funding universities. Concurrently, they set a target of increasing the proportion of students entering higher education to 50% by the year 2010. The initial fee of around £1,000 per year was insufficient to meet the funding needs of universities, leading to further proposals for reform.

Productive resources are essential components in an economy, contributing to its overall output and growth. When the government increases its spending, it may use resources that would have been allocated to the private sector. This can lead to a phenomenon known as "crowding out," where the increased government spending does not result in an increase in the total output of the economy. Opinions on the significance of crowding out vary among economists, with some considering it a perpetual concern and others viewing it as a minor issue, particularly during periods of economic depression. Critics of fiscal policy often refer to the concept of Ricardian equivalence, which posits that an increase in government debt will eventually necessitate higher future taxes to repay it. This expectation of future tax increases may lead individuals to reduce their current consumption and increase their savings to prepare for the higher taxes. Consequently, under Ricardian equivalence, any stimulus to demand from tax cuts may be counterbalanced by the increased savings intended to cover future tax liabilities. Income inequality is measured by the distribution of income among individuals, while wealth inequality is assessed by the distribution of wealth ownership. There are different forms of inequality, such as differences in consumption, land ownership, and human capital, and can be observed at different levels. The Gini coefficient is a widely recognized measure of income disparity among individuals. Another example is the Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index, a composite index that incorporates inequality considerations to provide a more comprehensive assessment of a country's development. Equity emphasizes fairness and justice in the distribution of resources and opportunities. Understanding and addressing economic inequality is crucial for promoting social cohesion and ensuring sustainable development.

The history of women in academia is marked by numerous milestones and achievements. One notable pioneer was the first recorded woman to earn a doctorate in science. She worked at the University of Bologna and became the first salaried female university teacher, at one point being the highest paid employee there. In 1732, she made history again by becoming the first woman member of a scientific establishment, when she was elected to the Academy of Sciences of the Institute of Bologna. The first state-financed higher education institution for women in Europe was established in 1764 by Catherine II of Russia. The Commission of National Education in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, founded in 1777, is considered the first Ministry of Education in history. It was a central, autonomous body responsible for nationwide, secular, and coeducational training. The late 19th century saw the emergence of the "Flying University" in the Russian province of Poland. This underground institution was created in response to the lack of higher education opportunities for women. Polish scholars and academics covertly taught women at this institution. Among its most famous students was Maria Skłodowska-Curie, better known as Marie Curie, who would later win two Nobel Prizes. Religious establishments provided education for women. Not all of the institutions focused on preparing women for marriage and motherhood. For example, the Quakers, from their foundation in the mid-17th century, held more egalitarian views on women, allowing for greater equality in education and other aspects of life. Outside of religious contexts, the Newington Academy for Girls was established in 1824 by abolitionists William Allen and his wife Grizell Hoare. This institution represented another step forward in providing educational opportunities for women, further challenging societal norms and expectations.

Dear Reader, We kindly request that you promptly complete and return the enclosed forms. The first form is for acknowledging any outstanding debts and listing the names of books covered by the statement, which should be filled out on the enclosed blank (blue blank). The second form is for updating our records (yellow blank). Lastly, please send us a postal money order for the amount of money you can spare at this time. We urge you to fill out and send the forms as soon as possible. On May 15, 1906, we received timely returns of money and acknowledgments, which were both encouraging and prompt. Surprisingly, some individuals who were initially considered doubtful were among the first to acknowledge their debts. Eventually, they were able to reproduce their books, and the acknowledged balances almost matched their estimated total of good accounts. Remittances continued until over $170,000 was paid. Approximately $25,000 of this amount covered accounts that were not included in their estimate of collectible indebtedness. This increased their estimated total to $200,000, confirming that more than eighty-five percent of all owed debts were acknowledged promptly under this call on honor. Four years later, we were pleasantly surprised to receive a check for $250 from a lawyer in Florida for a bill incurred long before, which we had no memory of. Let those who doubt the existence of ideals and lament the dishonesty of this materialistic age take note that money is not everything. It is also a reminder to those who grudgingly admit that there are a few honest men but no honest lawyers that even lawyers can possess a sense of honor. Some interesting instances of escape occurred during this time. A friend of mine, who lived on the Taylor Street side of Russian Hill, had a daughter who had lived in Japan and learned wise measures. When the earthquake struck, she immediately filled the bathtub with water. A nearby grocery store, which was doomed, asked customers to help themselves to goods. My friend chose a dozen large siphon bottles of soda water. The house was detached and initially escaped the fire, but eventually, the roof caught fire from flying embers, and the fire began to spread slowly. When it was time to leave the house, a large American flag was raised on a conspicuous staff. A company of soldiers from the Presidio, who were on general duty, saw the flag several blocks away and made their way to the house to save the colors. Upon finding the bathroom water supply, they mixed it with sand and plastered the burning spots. They managed to arrest the spreading flames but could not reach the fire under the cornice. Then they utilized the siphon bottles; one soldier, held by his legs, hung over the roof and squirted the small stream on the crucial spot. The danger was soon over, and the house was saved, along with a group of others that would have burned with it. While many individuals never fully recovered their property or their nerve, it is certain that a new spirit was generated. Great obstacles were overcome, and determination was invincible. We were forced to act broadly, and we reversed the negative policy of doing nothing and owing nothing. We went into debt with our eyes open and spent millions in money for the public good. The city was made safe and beautiful. The City Hall, the Public Library, and the Auditorium make our Civic Center a source of pride. The truly great exposition of 1915 was carried out in a way that increased our courage and our capacity. We have developed a fine public spirit and efficient cooperation. We need fear nothing in the future. We have character and are gaining in capacity. Throughout my residence in San Francisco, vocation and avocation have about equally divided my time and energy. I have done some things because I was obliged to and many others because I wished to. When one is fitted and trained for a specific task, they are likely to devote themselves steadily and profitably to it. However, when one is an amateur and not a master, they are sure to be handicapped. After about a year in the Indian department, a change in administration left me without a job. For about a year, I worked as a bookkeeper for a stock-broker. Then, for another year, I was a money-broker, selling currency, silver, and revenue stamps. When that business dwindled, I was ready for anything. A friend had loaned money to a printer and seemed about to lose it. In 1867, I became a bookkeeper and assistant in this printing office to rescue the loan, and eventually succeeded. I liked the business and had the courage to buy a small interest, borrowing the necessary money from a bank at one percent a month. I knew very little about the art and even less about business. It meant years of struggling to meet the weekly payroll, often in fear of the sheriff, but I stuck to it and gradually established a good business. I found satisfaction in production and had many pleasant experiences.

Project management is a critical process that involves planning, organizing, and overseeing the various aspects of a project to ensure its successful completion. It requires a high level of expertise in the specific domain the project is focused on. Project managers must be adept at handling all aspects of a project, from inception to completion. One of the key responsibilities of a project manager is to adapt to the internal procedures of the client and establish strong relationships with the nominated representatives. This is essential in ensuring that the project meets its objectives in terms of cost, time, quality, and, most importantly, client satisfaction. There are several key topics that project managers need to focus on, including: 1. Specifying the reason why a project is important and its overall objectives. 2. Defining the quality of the deliverables and the expected outcomes. 3. Estimating the resources required for the project, including人力, materials, and finances. 4. Developing a timescale and investment plan for the project. 5. Securing corporate agreement and funding for the project. 6. Implementing a management plan to guide the project team. 7. Building and motivating the project team. 8. Conducting risk assessments and managing changes in the project scope. 9. Monitoring and maintaining the project's progress. 10. Managing stakeholders, providers, and other external parties involved in the project. 11. Closing the project once it has been completed. Project management tools, knowledge, and techniques are often unique to the field. Some examples include work breakdown structures, critical path analysis, and earned value management. However, understanding and applying these tools and techniques alone is not sufficient for effective project management. A project manager must possess knowledge and skills from at least four areas of expertise: 1. Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK): A comprehensive guide that outlines the best practices in project management. 2. Application Area Knowledge: Understanding the specific domain or industry the project is focused on. 3. Standards and Regulations: Familiarity with the standards and regulations set forth by organizations such as the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) for project management. 4. General Management Skills: Proficiency in areas such as leadership, communication, and decision-making. 5. Project Environment Management: The ability to manage the project's environment, including its internal and external factors. In summary, effective project management requires a combination of expertise, adaptability, and the use of appropriate tools and techniques. By focusing on the key topics and leveraging their knowledge and skills, project managers can ensure the successful completion of their projects while meeting the objectives and expectations of all stakeholders involved.

The case in question involved a debate over the use of certifications from organizations such as the National Board of Trial Advocacy (NBTA) on a lawyer's letterhead. The court's decision was split, with various justices offering their own perspectives. The plurality opinion did not find justification for banning certifications from legitimate organizations like the NBTA. They believed that the use of such certifications did not inherently mislead the public. Justice Marshall, in his concurring opinion, agreed that the letterhead in question was not misleading in its actual use. However, he noted that the ruling against the use of the NBTA certification should be overturned. He was concerned that a misimpression could be created that the organization is a federal agency. While most lawyers are aware that the federal government does not regulate lawyers, the general public may not share this knowledge. Justice White, in his dissenting opinion, concurred with Marshall's view that the letterhead could be potentially misleading. However, he disagreed on the approach, stating that it should be the responsibility of the petitioner to clarify their advertisement and remove any potential for misunderstanding. Justice O'Connor, joined by Justices Rehnquist and Scalia, offered a dissenting opinion as well. They argued that the regulation of attorneys should be left to the states. The Supreme Court of Illinois, being responsible for monitoring the legal profession within the state, is in a better position to determine which statements may be misleading. They believe that the state courts are the final arbiters on whether a statement is misleading or not. This case highlights the complexities of professional regulation and the differing views on how to best protect the public from potential misinformation. It underscores the importance of clear communication and transparency in the legal profession.

Jainism, as a religious community, has been a subject of debate regarding its status as a minority in India. Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister of India, acknowledged the presence of various religious minorities, including Jains, in his speech on September 3, 1949. He emphasized that India could not be considered a Hindu Rashtra, as it would imply that minorities were not full citizens of the country. The Indian Constitution, in Article 25, guarantees the fundamental right to freedom of religion. Jainism, along with Buddhism and Sikhism, is mentioned in Explanation II of this article, recognizing it as a distinct religion. Nehru further assured a Jain delegation in a letter dated January 31, 1950, that they should have no concerns about their constitutional position. The second stanza of the Indian National Anthem, "Jana Gana Mana," also acknowledges Jainism as a separate religious denomination, alongside Hinduism, Islam, and other religions. However, the Indian Supreme Court ruled in 2005 that Jains, Sikhs, and Buddhists are part of the broader Hindu fold, as they are Indic religions and interconnected, despite being distinct religions. In 1993, the National Minorities Commission recommended that the Jain community be declared a minority religious community. The fundamental differences in philosophy between Jainism and other religions were taken into account in the recommendation. In summary, while the status of Jainism as a minority religion in India has been a topic of discussion, it is recognized as a distinct religious community within the broader Hindu fold, with its own unique beliefs and practices.

Curiosity, a fundamental aspect of human nature, is often associated with the desire to learn and understand the world around us. It can be observed in various fields such as algebra, morals, politics, natural philosophy, and more. This innate curiosity is not limited to abstract concepts but also extends to the real connections and existence of ideas. In addition to the pursuit of knowledge, there exists a distinct form of curiosity that is driven by a different principle. This form is characterized by an insatiable desire to know about the actions and circumstances of others, even when there is no direct personal interest involved. This type of curiosity often relies on information provided by others, rather than self-directed study or application. In 1954, psychologist Daniel Berlyne further differentiated curiosity into two types: perceptual curiosity and epistemic curiosity. Perceptual curiosity is driven by the need to explore novel stimuli, while epistemic curiosity is the desire to understand and learn new information. In 2004, a psychometric scale was developed to assess both epistemic and perceptual curiosity, providing a more nuanced understanding of this complex human trait. Intellectual Curiosity in Children Children are naturally curious beings, and their intellectual curiosity can be influenced by the responses they receive from their parents. When parents consistently react negatively to their children's questions, it can discourage them from asking questions and exploring new ideas, potentially stifling their curiosity. Conversely, when parents respond positively to their children's inquiries, it can encourage them to continue asking questions and seeking knowledge, fostering a greater sense of curiosity. Academic Performance Intellectual curiosity plays a significant role in academic performance. Students who exhibit a strong desire to learn and understand new concepts are more likely to engage with the material, leading to better academic outcomes. This curiosity can also drive students to pursue further education and explore new areas of study, contributing to their overall intellectual development.

An ancient Greek analogue computer is used to predict eclipses and positions in the sky. It is believed to have been designed around 100 BC and is a sophisticated example of angular rotations, translating the angle between celestial bodies into the rotation of the device. The mechanism requires a differential gear, a gearing arrangement that sums or differences two angular inputs. In 2008, scientists reported new findings in the journal Nature, showing that the Antikythera mechanism not only tracked the Metonic calendar and predicted solar eclipses, but also calculated the timing of panhellenic athletic games, such as the ancient Olympic Games. The names of the months used on calendars from Epirus in northwestern Greece and the island of Corcyra are similar on the instrument. The rear face of the Antikythera mechanism features five dials. The two large displays are the Metonic and the Saros dials, while the three smaller indicators are the Olympiad Dial (renamed the Games dial), the Callippic, and the exeligmos. The Metonic dial is the main upper dial on the rear of the mechanism. The Metonic cycle, defined in several physical units, consists of 235 synodic months, which is very close (to within less than 13 one-millionths) to 19 tropical years. This makes it a convenient interval for converting between lunar and solar calendars. The Metonic dial covers 235 months in five rotations, following a spiral track with a follower on the pointer that keeps track of the layer of the spiral. The Antikythera mechanism remains a remarkable testament to the advanced knowledge and technological capabilities of the ancient Greeks. Its discovery has provided valuable insights into the history of astronomy, mathematics, and engineering.

This paper presents a novel approach for efficient simulation of light transport in participating media, introducing the time-dependent integral-form of the radiative transfer equation to the computer graphics community. Our method leverages spatial density estimation techniques and high-density continuous photon trajectories to significantly mitigate the variance of transient light transport simulation, enabling the rendering of complex effects such as multiple scattering and caustics. Our contributions are significant for transient imaging, where emerging techniques and hardware advances demand reliable transient data under controlled setups. Our method provides a robust solution for efficiently obtaining this data, which can be used to gain valuable insights into transient light transport. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through various scenes, including the Cornell spheres, Mirrors, Pumpkin, and Juice scenes, showing its ability to handle complex caustics and different media properties. The innovative aspects of our research include the derivation of a new progressive scheme that extends density estimators to account for light time-of-flight, and the computation of the method's convergence with optimal asymptotic convergence rates. Our results show that combining continuous photon trajectories in transient state with our optimal spatio-temporal convergence rates allows for robust computation of noise-free solutions to the time-resolved RTE for complex light paths. In the future, we aim to conduct a more thorough analysis of variance reduction and bias impact in transient state under varying media characteristics. Transient-state adaptation of higher-dimensional photon estimators and hybrid techniques could be used to improve the performance of time-resolved rendering for a general set of geometries and media characteristics.

Allyl halides are a class of organic compounds that incorporate an allyl group, which is a structure consisting of a carbon atom double-bonded to two other carbon atoms, with the formula (CH2=CH-CH2). This functional group is attached to a halogen atom, creating a variety of allyl halides. The most common allyl halides include: - Allyl chloride (3-chloro-1-propene), with the chemical formula CH2=CH-CH2Cl. The chemical formula CH2 is used for Allyl bromide. The chemical formula CH2 is used for Allyl iodide (3-iodo-1-propene). - Allyl fluoride (3-fluoro-1-propene), with the chemical formula CH2=CH-CH2F. These compounds are widely used in organic synthesis and as intermediates in the production of various chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Allyl halides are known for their reactivity, particularly in reactions such as nucleophilic substitution and addition to double bonds. For further reading and exploration, you may also want to look into pages related to the allyl group and its various applications in chemistry.

The paper focuses on models that represent the feedback between an operator and an integrator, a structure that is prevalent in biophysical models of neuronal circuits. The integrator in these models symbolizes the neuronal membrane, while the fading memory operator encapsulates the complex dynamics of ion channels' input-output relationship. A paramount challenge in system identification arises when feedback disrupts the fading memory property, as is common in observed neuronal behaviors such as excitability and oscillations. The paper introduces a novel parametrization approach to identify such systems by leveraging the series interconnection of Generalized Orthonormal Basis Functions (GOBFs) combined with a static Artificial Neural Network (ANN) nonlinearity, which is posited as a universal approximator for fading memory operators. This methodology is particularly innovative as it addresses the难点 of identifying feedback systems that lack fading memory, where traditional guarantees on system behavior are typically elusive. The paper's contributions are manifold: it reformulates the neuronal system identification within the framework of fading memory operator identification, provides a proof of the universal approximation capability of the proposed model structure, and offers a heuristic for selecting GOBF poles based on the input-output property of ultrasensitivity, which is critical for neuronal systems. The structure of the paper is methodically outlined, beginning with the formulation of the identification problem and an argument for the generality of the model class used. Subsequent sections present the proof of the model's universal approximation properties and discuss the pole selection heuristic for neuronal systems. An illustrative example of identifying a bursting neuronal model using the proposed model structure is also provided. This paper presents a significant advancement in the field of system identification by introducing a novel parametrization approach that promises to enhance the accuracy and reliability of system modeling.

This section delves into the intricacies of defect density scaling during a slow quench in critical systems, particularly highlighting the distinction between quenches through a critical line versus a critical point. The authors propose a general conclusion derived from a $d$-dimensional model with $z= u=1$, showcasing how the defect density scales with the quench rate, $\tau$, and is influenced by the dimensionality of the critical surface traversed during the quench. The innovative aspect of this research is the formulation of a scaling law for defect density applicable to arbitrary critical systems, encapsulated in the equation \( n \sim 1/\tau^{m u/(z u+1)} \), which elegantly generalizes previous results and offers new insights into the behavior of defect densities in various dimensions and critical exponents. Furthermore, the paper explores the correlation of defects in a 2D system, introducing operators that measure the correlation between defects produced during the quench. The authors demonstrate that the correlation function can be calculated similarly to the 1D case, and provide an expression for the expectation value of the correlation operator in terms of the Majorana fermion operators. A key result is the derivation of the correlation function in the post-quench state, revealing the spatial anisotropy of the defect correlation function, even for equal couplings \( J_1 = J_2 \). The paper also presents a numerical evaluation of the correlation function, illustrating the anisotropic nature of defect correlations and their dependence on the quench rate. The language used in this section is clear and concise, facilitating an understanding of the complex phenomena under investigation. The results are presented in a manner that emphasizes the generalizability of the findings, making a significant contribution to the understanding of defect dynamics in critical systems. There is a visual representation of the theoretical predictions in the figures included in the paper.

During the Middle Ages, diets varied significantly between social classes. Poor families used to rely on grains and vegetables for soups and stew. They cultivated their own small plots of land to supplement their diet with local dairy products, cheaper meats like beef, pork, or lamb, and fish if accessible. Vegetables, herbs, fruits, nuts, and honey were also staples, sourced from their gardens or nearby natural resources. However, they could not afford spices and were legally restricted from hunting game such as deer, boar, or rabbits. The nobility and upper class enjoyed a richer diet. Their meals were an elaborate display of colors and flavors, often served in small portions—a trend influenced by cultural factors of the time. A variety of meats such as venison, pork, and lamb, fish and shellfish, an assortment of spices, cheese, fruits, and a limited range of vegetables were included in the upper class diet. Many of the spices used in these foods were imported from outside Europe. Spices were a common element in the diets of all social classes, albeit with variations. While the lower class primarily used local and home-grown spices, the wealthier classes indulged in exotic, imported spices. As living standards improved over time, even the lower classes in urban areas began to enjoy a more varied diet, including spices that were previously unaffordable or inaccessible. Overall, the Middle Ages saw a clear distinction in dietary habits between the rich and the poor, with the former enjoying a more diverse and luxurious diet compared to the latter's more basic and locally sourced food. However, as time progressed, even the lower classes experienced improvements in their diet, reflecting a gradual increase in living standards.

The origin of cosmic rays remains a mystery a century after their discovery. Supernova remnants (SNRs) are considered potential sources, but whether they can act as cosmic-ray PeVatrons is still uncertain. The connection between cosmic-ray physics and very high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray astronomy is strong, as SNRs should emit VHE gamma rays due to the decay of neutral pions produced in interactions between accelerated cosmic rays and swept-up gas. Evidence for this has been found at GeV energies, and several SNRs are known gamma-ray emitters at TeV energies. However, distinguishing between hadronic and leptonic processes in gamma-ray emission is challenging. Observing SNRs in the >10 TeV energy domain could provide crucial insights, as detection of an SNR spectrum extending to ~100 TeV would indicate hadronic emission and PeVatron status. The Key Science Project aims to search for PeVatrons using a telescope. The strategy includes deep observations of known sources with hard spectra and hints of multi-TeV spectral extension, as well as searching for diffuse gamma-ray emission around prominent SNRs. The latter is based on the expectation that PeV particles escape the SNR shock and propagate diffusively, producing gamma rays through interactions with ambient gas. The SNR RX J1713.7-3946 is a prime target for this investigation, as its gamma-ray spectrum suggests that the highest energy particles may have escaped. The KSP's scientific objectives are to: 1. Determine where and how PeV rays are accelerated. 2. Determine if the rays form a uniform distribution or are concentrated in a specific area. 3. Map the distribution of PeVatrons in the Galaxy. 4. Investigate whether young shell-type SNRs accelerate hadronic cosmic rays to PeV energies. 5. Understand the energy limits and efficiency of this acceleration. The KSP will advance our understanding by: - Exploiting the tight connection between cosmic-ray studies and gamma-ray astronomy, especially the production of gamma rays during cosmic-ray acceleration. - Leveraging CTA's superior sensitivity and spectroscopic capability compared to previous instruments, allowing detection of the most energetic photons and sampling of the highest energy particles in the Galaxy. - Focusing on observations that can resolve the ambiguity between leptonic and hadronic origins at energies above 50 TeV, where the Klein-Nishina effect suppresses leptonic emission. The KSP will perform dedicated observations of sources detected in the CTA Galactic Plane Survey with hard power-law spectra extending to extremely high energies. These observations will measure the spectrum extension, provide precise localization, and identify multi-wavelength counterparts, pinpointing the origin of PeVatrons. Discovering even one Galactic PeVatron would be a significant breakthrough, revealing the physics of the most extreme accelerators in the Galaxy. The project's high-risk/high-gain nature and the importance of developing the Small-Sized Telescope array make it a fitting candidate for a Key Science Project.

This section presents a comprehensive exploration of the cross-world counterfactual error (CWCE) within the framework of structural causal models (SCMs). The authors derive mathematical expressions for the joint distribution of cross-world potential outcomes and the distribution of the CWCE, highlighting the conditions under which these expressions simplify. The innovative aspects of this research are evident in the detailed derivation of these distributions, which are expressed in terms of observed data associations and conditional distributions of noise and receptiveness factors given the factual data. The paper's contributions are further underscored by the exploration of specific examples, including Gaussian linear mixed models and Log-normal linear mixed models. These examples serve to illustrate the theoretical findings and provide practical insights into the behavior of the CWCE under different scenarios. The authors demonstrate that the CWCE distribution can be Gaussian or Log-normal, depending on the model, and that its variance is influenced by an individual's exposure history. In the Gaussian linear mixed model example, the authors show that the CWCE is a linear combination of components of a multivariate Gaussian distributed random variable, leading to a Gaussian distribution for the CWCE itself. The variance of the CWCE is shown to depend on the exposure history, with more exposure leading to less variable CWCE distributions as more information about the individual's receptiveness factors is learned. The Log-normal linear mixed model example reveals that the CWCE distribution can be highly variable, especially with fewer repeats. However, as the number of repeats increases, the majority of the probability mass moves away from the average causal effect (ACE), providing more information about the receptiveness factors. The paper also addresses the importance of knowing the confounder distribution in the population to derive the distribution of the individual causal effect (ICE) in the Log-normal linear mixed assignment scenario. This underscores the practical implications of the research and the need for careful consideration of population-level factors. The methodology for further research and application is accessible thanks to the software code written in R by the authors. The figures included in the paper effectively visualize the distributions of the CWCE for different individuals based on varying numbers of repeats, providing a clear and concise representation of the theoretical findings. In summary, this section of the paper offers a significant contribution to the understanding of the CWCE within SCMs, providing both theoretical derivations and practical examples that enhance the reader's comprehension of this complex topic. The clear language and detailed explanations make the paper accessible to a wide audience, while the innovative aspects of the research are emphasized through the exploration of different causal models and the derivation of the CWCE distributions.

This has led to the development of various options for securing health care directives, which can be particularly valuable in situations where a patient's decision-making capacity may be compromised due to factors such as immaturity, mental illness, or severe brain damage. In light of these considerations, the council has released a comprehensive report aimed at expanding upon previous guidelines and exploring the key features of a meaningful and effective physician-proxy relationship. The report begins by defining several key terms related to health care directives, providing a solid foundation for understanding the various aspects of this complex issue. Building upon this foundation, the report delves into the theoretical frameworks that guide decision-making for patients who are unable to make their own health care choices. This includes a detailed examination of the spectrum of decision-making capacity, which ranges from immaturity to mental illness and serious brain damage. The protocol for identifying a surrogate decision-maker is one of the key components of the report. The report provides clear guidance for physicians on how to navigate this process, as well as how to address potential conflicts that may arise between the surrogate and the medical team. In addition to addressing the practical aspects of surrogate decision-making, the report also offers valuable insights into nurturing an effective physician-proxy relationship. This includes strategies for fostering open communication, building trust, and ensuring that the patient's best interests are always at the forefront of the decision-making process. To further enhance the understanding of this critical issue, the report also presents the findings of a study that sought to describe physicians' experiences with surrogate communication and decision-making for hospitalized adults. The study provides valuable insights into the challenges and opportunities associated with this aspect of patient care, offering a unique perspective on the complexities of surrogate decision-making. In summary, the council's report on end-of-life decisions and surrogate decision-making offers a thorough and nuanced exploration of this important topic. By providing clear definitions, theoretical frameworks, and practical guidance, the report serves as a valuable resource for physicians, patients, and all those involved in the complex process of making health care decisions for individuals with diminished decisional faculties.

The geometric transversals and the largest rectangles were discussed in 2017). We present a novel approach to model the dynamics of VEGF-A signaling pathways, focusing on the formation and dissociation of receptor complexes, and the phosphorylation process. Our methodology is based on the use of matrix-analytic techniques, which allow for efficient computation of important descriptors of the system's behavior, such as the time to reach a certain number of phosphorylated complexes and the stationary distribution of the process. The binding and unbinding of monomers are considered instantaneous reactions in our first model. We derive a system of equations that can be solved recursively to obtain the moments of the process, thus avoiding the need for direct calculation of the inverse of a large matrix. This approach is detailed in Algorithm 1, which is provided in Appendix C. The long-term behavior of the system is characterized by the stationary distribution, which can be computed using Algorithm 2, also listed in Appendix C. The mean number of complexes in the steady state is then easily obtained from this distribution. The second model extends the first by considering the phosphorylation of dimers as a separate reaction rather than an instantaneous step. We can evaluate the impact of including phosphorylation as an independent reaction on the system's behavior. The matrix-analytic approach resulted in a three-dimensional continuous-time Markov chain. The level structure of the state space is used to efficiently compute the moments of the absorption time in an auxiliary CTMC, as well as the stationary distribution of the process. The third model incorporates the competition between VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 for binding to VEGF-A. While both receptors are expressed on endothelial cells, VEGFR1 has a higher binding affinity but may act as a decoy, preventing VEGF-A from binding to VEGFR2, which is essential for endothelial cell homeostasis. This model accounts for the different copy numbers of VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 in various cell lines and considers the distinct signaling pathways they induce. A framework that can efficiently analyze the dynamics of complex formation and dissociation is provided by our research. The matrix-analytic approach allows for the computation of key descriptors of the system's behavior, offering insights into the role of different receptors and the impact of phosphorylation on the signaling process. Additional reactions and details of the signaling pathways can be incorporated into the models and algorithms presented here.

Among UWB techniques, Impulse Radio-based UWB (IR-UWB) stands out due to its superior performance and complexity trade-offs \cite{Win1998}. High time resolution and narrow impulse signals make IR-UWB systems ideal for positioning and ranging. Recent advancements in Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) technology have facilitated the digital representation of IR-UWB pulses, with high-speed ADCs capable of achieving a signal-to-noise and distortion ratio (SNDR) exceeding $30~\mb{dB}$ for a bandwidth of $10~\mb{GHz}$ \cite{murmann-adc-survey}. The way for digital designs has been paved by this progress. To maximize the use of regulatory specifications, transceivers should operate within the $3.1-10\,\mb{GHz}$ range or in the unlicensed millimeter wave (mmWave) frequency band \cite{fcc2002}. In this work, we propose a transceiver structure that can be adapted for multiple applications, enhancing the utilization of the transceiver infrastructure.
